title: Stoic in success
hook: the horse is handsome, not you

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic in illness, prohairesis, the leg hindered and the will still free. Your line was not the will. What kind thing did you do for your body? Day six hundred eighty-two.

The promotion comes through. Or the grade, or the offer on the house, or the post that suddenly has ten thousand likes. For a day or two, you walk differently. You catch yourself rereading the congratulations. You're a little more confident in meetings, a little less patient with people who haven't had your luck. Nobody warns you about this part. We get plenty of advice about failure, and almost none about winning. The Stoics thought success was a test too, sometimes a harder one. Today: Stoic in success.
screen: `THE PROMOTION COMES THROUGH.` → `REREADING THE CONGRATULATIONS.` → `WINNING IS A TEST TOO.`

segments.voice: First, the horse. Early this year we met Epictetus's line from the Handbook: don't take pride in any excellence that isn't yours. If a horse were proud and said, I'm handsome, that could be borne. But when you say, I have a handsome horse, you're proud of the horse's good, not your own. In success, a lot of what we're proud of is horse: the title, the money, the numbers, the luck of timing. What's yours is the effort, the honesty, how you treated people on the way. Second, a warning Marcus wrote to himself. In book six, he tells himself: take care not to be Caesarified, not to be dyed in that color. He was the most powerful man in the Roman world, and he could feel the purple seeping in. The Greek is a single word he seems to have coined, apokaisarōthēs, and it's almost funny, as if becoming Caesar were a disease you could catch. Third, how to hold a win. Marcus describes, in book eight, a way of having good things: receive them without arrogance, and let them go easily. He'd watched his adoptive father, Antoninus Pius, use the comforts of power without showing off and without fussy refusals, enjoying them when present and not missing them when gone. Fourth, why this matters. Success changes how we see other people. It's easy to start thinking the win proves we're better. The Stoics would say: you're the same person you were last week, with a different horse. Enjoy the horse. Thank the people who helped. Stay kind to those still waiting for theirs.
screen: `PROUD OF THE HORSE, NOT YOURSELF.` · `DON'T BE CAESARIFIED.` · `RECEIVE WITHOUT ARROGANCE.` · `THE SAME PERSON, A DIFFERENT HORSE.` · then, large: `NOT MY HORSE.`

segments.voice: Think of one recent win, small or large. Let yourself feel glad about it; that's allowed. Now sort it gently. What part was the horse: luck, timing, other people's help, things given to you? What part was yours: effort, honesty, care? Hold both. Then think of one person who helped make the win happen. Picture thanking them. Finally, picture someone still waiting for their own win, and how you might treat them this week. The bell holds the time.
Antoninus Pius, whom Marcus watched use the comforts of power without showing off and without missing them when they were gone. Today's word.
Your line: not my horse. When you feel proud today, ask whether it's you or the horse, and thank someone who helped. Day six hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet a success by separating what was luck or help from their own effort, thanking those who helped, and watching for arrogance.

original.note: Greek, Meditations 6.30: don't be Caesarified, a word Marcus seems to have coined.

trapdoor: what you thought: being Stoic in success means not enjoying it.
what it means: enjoy it, but know what's luck and what's yours, and don't let it make you arrogant.
what a scholar hears: Handbook 6 on the horse; Meditations 6.30 coins apokaisarōthēs; 8.33 says receive without arrogance, let go readily; 1.16 describes Antoninus Pius's ease with comforts.
